title: Transactions and durability: Gray 1981, and who actually coined ACID

claims.text: Jim Gray presented The Transaction Concept: Virtues and Limitations at the seventh Very Large Data Bases conference in Cannes in September 1981, describing transactions in terms of atomicity, defined as an all-or-nothing property, consistency, and durability, the survival of a committed transaction's effects after failures. He compared the transaction concept to a legal contract, in which work can proceed provisionally before a commitment establishes the resulting state. His earlier Notes on Data Base Operating Systems of 1978 had already covered concurrency control, locking, recovery, logging, checkpointing and commit protocols.

source.title: Jim Gray, The Transaction Concept: Virtues and Limitations, Proceedings of the 7th International Conference on Very Large Data Bases, Cannes, September 1981, pages 144-154

claims.text: The acronym itself is not Gray's. It appears in Haerder and Reuter's 1983 paper Principles of Transaction-Oriented Database Recovery in ACM Computing Surveys, which built on the earlier transaction processing work including Gray's, and which provides a terminological framework for describing recovery schemes conceptually rather than in an implementation-dependent way.

source.title: Theo Haerder and Andreas Reuter, Principles of Transaction-Oriented Database Recovery, ACM Computing Surveys volume 15 number 4, December 1983, pages 287-317, doi 10.1145/289.291 — the paper in which the ACID acronym appears

claims.text: Gray received the 1998 ACM Turing Award for seminal contributions to database and transaction processing research and technical leadership in system implementation.

source.title: Jim Gray — recipient of the 1998 ACM A. M. Turing Award for seminal contributions to database and transaction processing research and technical leadership in system implementation
